title: The snake's gait
hook: the next stanzas move in a meter named for a snake's gliding motion

segments.voice: Yesterday, named by deeds: no one can tell all His names, so the wise name Him by His works. That was the end of Jaap's first stanza. Today, the hymn changes its walk. Day three hundred thirty-six, the end of a week.

Have you ever watched a snake cross a path? It doesn't step. It doesn't hop. It pours. A small ripple starts at the head and travels down the whole body, and the snake is somewhere else before you've decided whether to be scared. No jerks, no pauses, one smooth wave after another. Indian poets heard that motion in certain rhythms of words, and they gave one meter a name for it. When Jaap Sahib leaves its first stanza, it starts to move exactly like that. Today: the snake's gait.
screen: `A SNAKE CROSSES THE PATH.` → `IT DOESN'T STEP. IT POURS.` → `A RHYTHM NAMED FOR THAT MOTION.`

segments.voice: The meter is called bhujang prayat. Bhujang is a snake. Prayat means going, moving. So, the snake's going, the snake's gait. It's an old meter of Sanskrit poetry, and Guru Gobind Singh uses it for long stretches of Jaap. Here's how it works. It's built from little groups of three syllables, and every group goes the same way: short, long, long. Da, DUM, DUM. Listen to the opening of the second stanza: na-mas-tvam, a-kaa-le. Short, long, long. Short, long, long. Then: na-mas-tvam, kri-paa-le. And the next: na-mas-tvam, a-roo-pe. Then: na-mas-tvam, a-noo-pe. Once you hear it, you can't stop hearing it. Each group is a small wave, and the waves keep rolling, line after line, the way a snake's body carries one ripple into the next. Why does the rhythm matter in a prayer? Because Jaap is meant to be said, out loud, often fast, often from memory, often by a whole room together. A steady meter is what lets a whole room glide through salutation after salutation without losing its place. The rhythm carries the words, so the mind is free to carry the meaning. And this is where the week ends. A few days ago you stood at the lookout. Since then you've met Jaap, the Tenth Guru's morning praise; the One with no mark and no caste; the king of kings above every throne; and the names drawn from deeds. Now the hymn begins to glide.
screen: `BHUJANG: SNAKE. PRAYAT: GOING.` · `SHORT, LONG, LONG: ONE SMALL WAVE.` · `NAMASTVAM AKAALE, NAMASTVAM KRIPAALE.` · `THE RHYTHM CARRIES THE WORDS.` · then, large: `GLIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read four lines in rhythm. Say them slowly first, tapping your knee on each long syllable. Namastvam akaale. Namastvam kripaale. Namastvam aroope. Namastvam anoope. Short, long, long. Now say them once more, a little faster, and let them run together like one long wave. Don't worry about the meaning yet; that's the next few days. Then stop, and let your breath find its own smooth rhythm, in and out, no jerks, no pauses. The bell holds the time.
Bhujang prayat. The snake's gait: a meter of short, long, long waves that Jaap Sahib glides in for long stretches.
Your line: glide. Today, pick one ordinary task, walking, washing up, typing, and do it in a smooth, unhurried rhythm, no jerks. Day three hundred thirty-six. A week, done.

original.note: Gurmukhi: bhujang, a snake; with prayat, going, it names the gliding meter of Jaap.

trapdoor: what you thought: the snake's gait is a strange title for a prayer.
what it means: it's the name of a meter whose short-long-long waves glide like a snake's body.
what a scholar hears: bhujangaprayata is a classical Sanskrit meter of four yagana feet (short-long-long) per quarter; Jaap uses it from stanza 2 on.
